strengths: Novel and elegant architectural idea that adapts asymmetric Siamese design (predictor + stop-gradient) from negative-free SSL to the single-branch test-time entropy minimization setting, without requiring augmentations, extra backbone passes, or teacher models — a non-trivial adaptation given the different objective (entropy vs. similarity) and single forward-pass constraint.

Extremely comprehensive empirical evaluation: 5 vision backbones (CNN and Transformer, various sizes) across multiple challenging TTA scenarios (label-shift, mixed corruption, batch-size=1, blind-spot subset, noise-resistance, mild scenario), plus LLM reasoning tasks (Math-500, CollegeMath, AIME24, Minerva) with Llama3.1-8B, showing broad applicability beyond vision.

Strong and consistent performance gains, especially in adversarial/stress-test settings (blind-spot adaptation, learning-from-noise) where prior SOTA methods (Tent, SAR, EATA, DeYO, COME) catastrophically collapse below the no-adaptation baseline, while ZeroSiam remains stable.
Negligible computational overhead (same GPU time as Tent, much faster than SAR/DeYO/COME) due to the single-pass design, making it practical for real-world deployment.

Thoughtful theoretical analysis (Theorem 1 with supporting lemmas) that provides intuition for why the asymmetric predictor absorbs biased gradients and prevents collapse, complementing the empirical evidence with a plausible mechanistic explanation.

Thorough ablations covering predictor architecture choices, learning-rate sensitivity, divergence loss choices, plug-and-play integration with existing TTA methods, and necessity of stop-gradient, which strengthen the credibility of the design choices.

Good positioning relative to both TTA and SSL literature, correctly identifying the shared collapse challenge and clearly articulating why naive SSL-style asymmetry cannot be directly applied to entropy minimization.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis, while intuitively appealing, relies on fairly strong/convenient assumptions and some post-hoc justifications (e.g., 'in practice we set ηh = k·ηf with k>1, so there always exists a k such that |ΔH(p^o)|>|ΔH(p^r)|'), which weakens the rigor of the guarantees and makes Theorem 1 read more as a plausibility argument than a tight formal result.

Performance gains are not universally dominant — in several individual settings (e.g., ViT-Base in Table 2, or specific corruption types in Tables 3/6) DeYO, EATA, or COME are competitive with or occasionally exceed ZeroSiam, so the main advantage is more about consistency/stability across settings rather than uniform superiority.

The appendix experiment on 'saving a collapsed model' (Section E.3) reports recovery succeeding in only 4 of 7 domains, revealing a real limitation in the method's ability to escape collapse once it has occurred, which is somewhat downplayed in the main text.

No variance/error bars are reported despite the inherently stochastic and streaming nature of TTA (online batch order, small batch sizes), making it hard to assess the statistical significance of some reported gains.

Recent related sharpness/feature-regularization TTA methods (e.g., Niu et al. 2025a, cited in related work) are not included as baselines in the main comparison tables, leaving open whether ZeroSiam's gains hold against the most recent competitors.

The architectural novelty is somewhat incremental — it is essentially a direct, if clever, transplantation of the SimSiam predictor/stop-gradient trick into a single-branch setting, and the core contribution is more about problem reformulation and validation than a fundamentally new mechanism.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practical problem (collapse in test-time entropy minimization) with a simple, lightweight architectural fix that requires no augmentations or extra backbone passes, making it attractive for efficient deployment.

Extremely broad empirical evaluation: multiple architectures (ResNet50-GN, ViT-B/S, ConvNeXt-Tiny, Swin-Tiny), multiple wild test scenarios (label shift, mixed corruptions, batch size=1, blind-spot adaptation, noise-only pre-adaptation), a mild scenario, and an LLM reasoning setting (Llama3.1-8B on four math benchmarks).
Efficiency is explicitly verified (Table 1) and the method shows essentially no runtime overhead relative to Tent while incorporating a predictor and alignment loss.
Good set of ablations: predictor depth/randomness, learning-rate sensitivity heatmap, generality across divergence/objective choices (Table 10), and plug-and-play integration with EATA/DeYO.
Attempts a theoretical treatment (Lemmas 1-2, Theorem 1) to explain why the asymmetric design resists collapse and regularizes biased gradients, going beyond purely empirical justification.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis relies on numerous informal approximations (e.g., '≈' steps in the Hessian analysis near collapse, assuming a specific uniform spread for p_j) and loose chaining of inequalities; the final bound h_min can be vacuous or even negative depending on α, δ, and |C|, undermining the claimed guarantee of avoiding collapse.

No error bars, variance, or multiple-seed results are reported anywhere in the main paper or appendix, despite TTA being known to be sensitive to batch ordering/initialization; given the paper's central claim is about 'stability', the absence of variance statistics is a significant gap.

The core architectural idea (predictor + stop-gradient on duplicated features from a single encoder pass) is a relatively straightforward adaptation of SimSiam/BYOL asymmetry to the TTA setting; conceptual novelty is moderate even though the engineering instantiation is reasonably elegant.

Internal inconsistency: the main method initializes the predictor as identity for a 'warm start,' but the collapse-recovery experiment in Appendix E.3 requires a randomly perturbed (non-identity) initialization to work, and the main predictor ablation (Table 8) also shows random initialization alone already yields large gains—raising questions about how much of ZeroSiam's benefit is attributable to the specific identity warm-start design versus generic symmetry breaking.

Performance is not uniformly dominant: in several tables (e.g., Table 2 ViT-B, Table 9 ConvNeXt-Tiny) ZeroSiam is outperformed by DeYO or COME, so claims of consistent superiority are somewhat overstated relative to the data shown.

CollegeMath evaluation subsamples 1200 of 2818 questions without described sampling methodology, and LLM experiments use only a single model (Llama3.1-8B-Instruct), limiting generality claims for the reasoning results.

The 'blind-spot' and 'noise pre-adaptation' stress tests, while illustrative, are somewhat artificial constructions that may not reflect realistic deployment distributions, making it hard to judge real-world significance of the reported gains in these settings.

strengths: Addresses a well-known and practically important failure mode (collapse) in test-time entropy minimization, which limits the real-world usability of methods like Tent.

The proposed architectural fix is lightweight and efficient: it embeds asymmetry (predictor + stop-gradient) within a single forward pass, avoiding the extra backbone passes/augmentations required by traditional Siamese SSL methods, and the efficiency table (Table 1) shows negligible overhead versus baselines.

Very extensive empirical evaluation across multiple backbones (ResNet, ViT-Base/Small, ConvNeXt, Swin), multiple challenging TTA protocols (label shift, mixed-corruption, batch size=1, blind-spot adaptation, noise resistance), and even LLM mathematical reasoning tasks, showing consistent and often large improvements over strong recent baselines (SAR, EATA, DeYO, COME).

Thorough ablations (predictor design, learning-rate sensitivity, divergence choice, plug-in compatibility with EATA/DeYO, stop-gradient necessity, sensitivity of alpha) that help clarify which components matter and the robustness of the method to hyperparameters.

Provides both empirical diagnostics (logit norm, center dominance, predictor drift) and a theoretical analysis attempting to explain why the asymmetric architecture resists collapse and regularizes biased gradients, which is a nice complement to the engineering contribution.

Demonstrates a particularly striking result in the adversarial 'blind-spot' and noise-pretraining stress tests, where prior methods catastrophically collapse while ZeroSiam remains stable, which is a meaningful practical contribution for real-world deployment.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis (Theorem 1, Lemmas 1-2) relies on multiple strong/loose approximations (e.g., first-order Taylor-like approximations of the entropy Hessian near collapse, informal 'we obtain the following approximation' steps) rather than rigorous bounds; the practical implications of the theorem (e.g., the exact value or usefulness of h_min) are not clearly connected back to the empirical results beyond a qualitative narrative.

The core technical idea is a fairly direct transplant of the SimSiam/BYOL predictor+stop-gradient trick into a single-branch entropy-minimization setting; the novelty is mainly in the engineering adaptation (reusing the same feature/classifier) rather than a fundamentally new collapse-prevention mechanism.

Several baselines (e.g., COME for vision, implemented 'based on DeYO') are reimplemented by the authors rather than using official code/numbers, which raises reproducibility and fairness-of-comparison concerns.

No variance/error bars or multiple-seed results are reported for the large TTA tables, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of the (sometimes modest) gains, especially for small benchmarks like AIME24 (only 30 problems, so a '+10%' gain corresponds to just 3 problems).

The integration experiments (Table 9) show that combining ZeroSiam with EATA/DeYO does not always outperform ZeroSiam alone, and this discrepancy is acknowledged but not resolved, leaving an open question about how ZeroSiam interacts with sample-selection-based methods.
Vision evaluation is restricted to ImageNet-C only; broader distribution-shift benchmarks (e.g., CIFAR-10/100-C, real-world shifts) are not included, somewhat limiting the generality claims.
The CollegeMath subsampling (1200 of 2818 questions) and other dataset curation choices are not well justified, raising minor concerns about selection bias in the LLM reasoning evaluation.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear and practical problem (collapse in test-time entropy minimization) and proposes a simple, efficient architectural solution (predictor + stop-gradient) that requires only a single backbone pass, unlike traditional Siamese SSL designs, making it very lightweight (Table 1 shows negligible overhead vs. baselines like SAR/DeYO).

Extensive empirical evaluation across many models (ResNet50-GN, ViT-Base/Small, ConvNeXt-Tiny, Swin-Tiny, Llama3.1-8B) and diverse challenging scenarios (label shifts, batch size=1, mixed corruptions, blind-spot adaptation, noise resistance, mild scenario), consistently showing strong and stable improvements over multiple recent SOTA baselines (SAR, EATA, DeYO, COME, TLM).

Theoretical analysis (Theorem 1 with supporting lemmas) provides some formal grounding for why the asymmetric architecture prevents collapse and regularizes biased learning signals, complementing the empirical findings.

Thorough ablations: predictor design choices, sensitivity to learning rates and alpha, integration with prior methods as a plug-and-play module, generality across different self-training objectives and divergence terms, and comparison with multi-branch methods (SPA, REM, TTE) on both accuracy and efficiency.
The blind-spot and noise-resistance stress tests are compelling demonstrations of robustness beyond standard benchmarks, showing the method's practical value for safe real-world deployment.
Good reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, public models/datasets, and appendix with extensive implementation details are provided.
Extension to LLM reasoning tasks (Math-500, CollegeMath, AIME24, Minerva) demonstrates broader applicability beyond vision TTA.
weaknesses: The theoretical results rely on several strong/simplifying assumptions (e.g., Lipschitz continuity, smoothness, specific collapse-direction constructions, linearized approximations near p_c→1) that may not tightly reflect real network training dynamics; the practical significance of the theorem beyond providing qualitative intuition is unclear.

Some accuracy gains, while consistently positive, are occasionally modest (e.g., LLM reasoning results in Table 5 show small absolute gains on some benchmarks like Minerva, and CollegeMath improvements are under 1.5%), raising questions about statistical significance for those particular tasks (though Table I shows low variance for vision tasks).

The paper's core architectural idea (predictor + stop-gradient asymmetry) is directly adapted from SimSiam/BYOL; while the adaptation to single-branch entropy minimization is non-trivial and well-executed, the fundamental novelty is more incremental (applying an existing SSL principle to a new setting) than a completely new mechanism.

The collapse-recovery experiment (Appendix E.3) admits that recovery only succeeds in 4 out of 7 domains and lacks a clear mechanistic explanation, which is an honest but somewhat unresolved limitation.

Some hyperparameter choices (e.g., predictor learning rate scaling for different architectures, larger ηh on smaller models) still appear to require some manual tuning per architecture family despite claims of robustness, and the proposed data-free ηh selection method (Appendix E.6) is noted to fail for some architectures like ConvNeXt.

Comparisons with very recent multi-branch methods (SPA, REM, TTE) are relegated to the appendix and only partially compared (e.g., REM has missing ResNet50-GN results), which could be seen as somewhat incomplete positioning against contemporaneous alternatives.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and practical problem (collapse in test-time entropy minimization) and proposes a conceptually clean solution inspired by asymmetric SSL architectures (SimSiam/BYOL), adapted to the single-branch entropy setting via a single lightweight predictor plus stop-gradient within one backbone pass, avoiding the overhead of augmentations or extra encoder passes used in prior SSL-style designs.

Extensive empirical validation across 5 vision backbones (CNN and transformer, including collapse-prone tiny models) and many challenging TTA protocols (label-imbalance, mixed corruptions, batch size=1, blind-spot adaptation, noise-only pre-adaptation, mild scenario), as well as an LLM reasoning setting (Math-500, CollegeMath, AIME24, Minerva), showing fairly consistent gains over multiple strong baselines (Tent, SAR, EATA, DeYO, COME, TLM).

Efficiency is a clear practical advantage: Table 1 shows ZeroSiam matches Tent's latency while competitors (SAR, DeYO, COME, and especially multi-branch methods in the appendix) incur substantially higher time/memory costs.

Reasonably thorough ablations: predictor design/depth, plug-in compatibility with EATA/DeYO, sensitivity to learning rates and α, generality across divergence functions and self-training objectives (Table 10), and a statistical run with multiple seeds (Table I) showing lower variance than DeYO.

An attempt at theoretical grounding (Theorem 1, Lemmas 1-2) connecting the predictor to gradient filtering and stable equilibrium, which, while informal in places, provides an interpretable narrative for why the mechanism works beyond pure empiricism.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis, while extensive in the appendix, relies on multiple informal approximations treated as near-equalities (e.g., the asymptotic Hessian approximations in Lemma 2's proof, the first-order linearization steps in Theorem 1), and several steps gloss over rigor (e.g., claiming 'there always exists a k such that |ΔH(p^o)|>|ΔH(p^r)|' without a constructive bound, or the Lipschitz constant for H in the non-collapse region being used loosely). The theory reads more as a plausibility argument than a rigorous guarantee, which weakens the paper's claim of being 'theoretically grounded.'

Several baseline numbers appear suspiciously degenerate (e.g., DeYO at 0.1%-0.5% accuracy on ViT-Small/ConvNeXt-Tiny in multiple tables), which raises concerns about whether all baselines were adequately tuned for the newly introduced stress-test scenarios (blind-spot subset, noise pre-adaptation), potentially inflating ZeroSiam's apparent margin of improvement.

The core architectural novelty is fairly incremental — applying a known asymmetry mechanism (predictor + stop-gradient from SimSiam/BYOL) to a different single-branch setting — and the 'first to study asymmetry in TTA' framing may overstate the conceptual leap given how directly the mechanism is borrowed.

The method still requires per-architecture tuning of the predictor learning rate ηh (Appendix C.2 shows quite different ηh/ηf ratios across models), undermining the 'minimal tuning' narrative; the proposed data-free selection heuristic (Appendix E.6) is preliminary, acknowledged to fail for some architectures (e.g., ConvNeXt), and not integrated into the main experiments.

Comparison with more directly relevant recent multi-branch/consistency-based TTA collapse-prevention methods (SPA, REM, TTE) is relegated to a brief appendix discussion with a single small table (Table J) and incomplete results (REM missing for ResNet50-GN), despite these being the closest competing design philosophies; this limits confidence that ZeroSiam is state-of-the-art relative to the most relevant recent alternatives.

The LLM reasoning evaluation uses only a single model (Llama3.1-8B-Instruct) and relatively modest/noisy benchmarks (e.g., AIME24 has only 30 problems), making the generalization claims to 'large language model reasoning' somewhat preliminary despite being advertised as a major contribution.

Qualitative explanations in Section 3.2 (e.g., 'predictor as an effective absorber of biased shortcut signals') are based on a single model/corruption-type visualization (ResNet50-GN, Snow level 5) and are largely descriptive rather than causally verified, so the broader mechanistic claims rest on limited and somewhat cherry-picked evidence.

strengths: Novel and simple architectural idea: adapting the SimSiam/BYOL asymmetric predictor + stop-gradient mechanism to single-branch test-time entropy minimization without requiring augmentations or extra backbone passes, which is a non-trivial adaptation since prior SSL asymmetry methods rely on two augmented views and similarity objectives.

Extensive empirical validation across a wide variety of challenging test-time adaptation scenarios (label shift, mixed corruption, batch size 1, blind-spot adaptation, noise-only pre-adaptation, mild scenario) and across 5 vision backbones plus an LLM reasoning setting, with consistent and often large improvements over strong recent baselines (SAR, EATA, DeYO, COME).

Efficiency is a genuine strength: ZeroSiam achieves these gains with essentially the same latency/memory as Tent, unlike multi-branch methods (SPA, REM, TTE) that incur substantial extra compute, as shown clearly in Table 1 and Table J.

Reasonably thorough theoretical analysis (Theorem 1, Lemmas 1-2) under stated assumptions attempts to formally explain why the online branch is more collapse-prone and why the stop-gradient/alignment term stabilizes training, which is a plus compared to many empirical-only TTA papers.

Good set of ablations and sensitivity analyses (predictor design, learning rate heatmaps, alpha sensitivity, generality across divergence/objective combinations, stop-gradient necessity, statistical variance over seeds) that support robustness of the design choices and reduce concerns about cherry-picked hyperparameters.

The extension to LLM test-time reasoning incentivization (Math-500, CollegeMath, AIME24, Minerva) broadens the applicability story beyond vision TTA, showing the asymmetry idea generalizes to a different modality and task structure.
Honest discussion of limitations in Appendix E.3 (collapse-recovery works in only 4/7 domains) and Appendix E.11 comparing favorably but fairly to concurrent multi-branch methods.
weaknesses: Some of the theoretical claims rely on fairly strong/idealized assumptions (Lipschitz constants, smoothness, specific identity initialization, synchronized encoder updates) that may not hold precisely in practice (e.g., with momentum SGD, batch normalization updates, LoRA for LLMs); the practical predictive value of the theorem beyond qualitative intuition is somewhat limited.

The predictor learning rate ηh and its interaction with encoder learning rate ηf still require some hand-tuning per architecture (e.g., different ratios for ResNet50-GN vs Swin-Tiny in Table F/Figure F), and while a data-free heuristic is proposed in Appendix E.6, the authors themselves note it does not generalize to all architectures (e.g., ConvNeXt), slightly undercutting the 'no heavy tuning' claim.

The improvement margins vary quite a bit across benchmarks/models (e.g., modest gains on ViT-Base in several tables vs. very large gains on ConvNeXt-Tiny/Swin-Tiny), and the paper could more clearly characterize when/why ZeroSiam's benefit is large vs. marginal, beyond noting 'collapse-prone' models benefit more.

LLM reasoning experiments are on a single model (Llama3.1-8B-Instruct) and relatively small benchmarks (e.g., AIME24 has only 30 problems), so the reported gains (e.g., +10% on AIME24) carry high variance and the generality of the LLM result is less convincing than the vision results.

Comparison with closely related multi-branch/asymmetric TTA works (SPA, REM, TTE) is relegated to the appendix rather than the main text, even though these seem like the most directly relevant recent baselines; a reader relying only on the main paper would not see this important comparison.

The paper's framing of 'shortcuts learnable by an extremely simple network' as the operational definition of bias is somewhat informal and not tightly connected to the formal theoretical analysis, leaving a conceptual gap between the intuitive narrative (Section 3.2) and the rigorous theorem (Theorem 1).
